summary: Kate Cassada, a Forbes contributor, argues that standardized testing pervades K-12 schooling and asks what these tests measure and what their results mean. The article contrasts state assessments, which are criterion-referenced and not comparable across states, with NAEP, the national sample-based test that offers a basis for comparison. It also explains the difference between criterion-referenced and norm-referenced scoring and urges readers to interpret scores within their full context.
one_line: Forbes column explaining what K-12 standardized tests measure, how NAEP differs from state tests, and criterion- versus norm-referenced scoring.
key_facts: Kate Cassada's Forbes article 'Standardized Tests Fill K-12 Schools. What Purpose Do They Serve?' is dated Oct 21, 2023.
The article states that testing 'feels like it is everywhere, every day, all the time' in K-12 public education in the United States.
Schools are held by the federal Every Student Succeeds Act to 95% student participation rates for administered state tests.
The National Assessment of Educational Progress (NAEP), known as the Nation's Report Card, is administered and reported through the National Center for Education Statistics.
The article describes NCES as an independent and nonpartisan branch of the U.S. Department of Education, mandated by Congress to collect, analyze, and disseminate education information.
In Iowa, student assessments are known as the Iowa Statewide Assessment of Student Progress.
In Virginia, students take Standards of Learning tests, and in Massachusetts students participate in the Massachusetts Comprehensive Assessment System.
The article says Iowa's scores cannot be compared with Virginia or Massachusetts because students in each state are not taught or tested on the same curriculum.
NAEP is administered through a sampling of American public and private school students across all states and jurisdictions, offering results with national reach.
Main NAEP selects students by grade level (4, 8, 12) every two years, with mathematics and reading central to score reporting.
Long-term trend NAEP offers an extended view of reading and mathematics achievement for students at ages 9, 13, and 17, and is not reported by state.
Criterion-referenced tests such as NAEP and state-level tests are aligned with a set of academic standards, while norm-referenced scoring ranks students relative to one another.
The article states that only 1% of students can score in the 99th or the 50th percentile on norm-referenced assessments such as the California Achievement Test.
The article notes that an opt-out movement has existed for several years as some parents refuse to let students take tests not required for programmatic advancement or graduation.
